summary.text: 木 depicts a whole tree, with trunk, branches and roots understood as parts of one image.

formation.text: This is a pictograph: the graph represents a tree as a whole, without a separate sound component. An older account describes it as 屮 above roots, but a competing analysis treats the apparent resemblance to 屮 as insufficient to establish a separate component.

components.text: The entire graph is pictorial: its form is understood as a tree, including trunk, branches and roots. These are aspects of one image, not independently established components; the individual strokes cannot each be assigned to a particular part.

history.text: Oracle-script- and bronze-script-style forms are consistent with the whole-tree interpretation. The selected illustrations are modern redrawings, not images of specific dated inscriptions, so they do not establish a sequence of graphic changes or identify individual strokes as particular branches or roots.
The received Shuowen account parses the graph as 屮 above roots. A competing paleographic analysis rejects 屮 as an independent component and reads 木 as a complete picture of a tree.

uncertainties.text: The oracle-bone phrase 埶(藝)木 is interpreted as referring to planting trees, but the inscription rubbing was not checked. The selected redrawings do not represent particular dated inscriptions.
The traditional parsing as 屮 plus roots conflicts with the whole-tree analysis; 屮 is therefore not established as an independent component here.

senses.gloss: tree; use in a tree-planting phrase
senses.text: The oracle-bone phrase 埶(藝)木 is interpreted as referring to planting trees, supporting a tree-related use. This example does not show whether that use predates the wood or board use.
木枋 in a bronze inscription is interpreted as a wooden writing board, supporting a wood or timber use. Its exact date and chronology relative to the tree-planting phrase are unresolved.
Current meanings include ‘tree’, ‘wood’ or ‘lumber’, and ‘wooden’. The evidence does not establish a dated sequence connecting these senses.

In a Mawangdui manuscript passage, 木 is reported as a sound-based spelling for 沐. This borrows the graph for another word rather than extending the meaning ‘tree’ or ‘wood’; the first use of this spelling is unresolved.

limitations.text: The tree-planting and wooden-board examples do not establish which sense came first or a development from ‘tree’ to ‘wood’ or ‘timber’. Dictionary citations for other senses, including ‘coffin’, do not establish chronology.
Reported place and polity names may be proper names or graph loans; their relationship to the ordinary word for ‘tree’ is unresolved.
The Mawangdui reading supports a context-specific loan of 木 for 沐, but neither the text’s composition date nor the first use of this spelling is established.
